The implementation does make the full test suite pass (I traced every test case by hand and confirmed the outputs match), but it does so by adding behavior that is not covered by — and actually contradicts — the docstring, which the request explicitly said should be the source of truth.

Docstring rule 2 says a small word is lowercased "unless it is the first or the last word of `text`" — only two exceptions, based on the small word's position in the *whole string*. The diff adds a third, undocumented exception:

```python
after_colon = index > 0 and result[-1].endswith(":")
...
if is_first or is_last or after_colon:
    result.append(word.capitalize())
```

This `after_colon` branch exists purely to make `test_subtitle_after_colon` pass (`"a"` after `"field:"` is neither the first nor last word of the text, so per the literal docstring it should stay lowercase, yet the test expects `"A"`). Nothing in the docstring mentions colons, subtitle segments, or any punctuation-based reset of the first/last logic, so a reader relying on the docstring (as instructed) would not be able to predict this behavior, and the docstring is now an inaccurate description of what the function does.

It's also narrowly tailored rather than general: it only checks for a literal trailing `":"` on the *previous* word, not other punctuation, and doesn't generalize the "start of a new segment" idea consistently (e.g. it doesn't affect rule 1 or rule 3 words the same way it affects rule 2). That's a strong signal it was reverse-engineered from the one failing test rather than derived from a specification.

Please either:
1. Update the docstring to explicitly document the colon-subtitle exception so the code and docs stay in sync, or
2. Find a different way to satisfy the test that follows only the documented first/last-word rule (if that's actually possible), and raise the docstring/test conflict with the teammate if it isn't.

As-is, the code and its own docstring disagree, which is exactly what the request asked us to avoid.
